articles.body:
Australian state governments could sue tobacco companies for billions in public hospital and healthcare costs, under a proposal developed by a former barrister who helped legally establish that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer.

The South Australian government is formally seeking advice on the proposal, while other states are reviewing it.

Authored by Sydney Health Law research affiliate Neil Francey, the proposal argues the states could file proceedings in the federal court seeking up to $50bn in compensation for health costs, and to fund cancer screening programs and prevention measures.

It targets the dominant tobacco companies in Australia – British American Tobacco (BAT), Philip Morris and Imperial Brands – and their parent corporations overseas.

Francey is presenting the blueprint at the Clinical Oncology Society of Australia’s annual scientific meeting in Sydney on Thursday, arguing the companies could be held liable for decades of misleading and deceptive conduct under Australian consumer law.

He has also briefed state government MPs. Under the plan, the six state governments would pool their resources to set up a dedicated, joint legal taskforce to run the case.

“For decades, the tobacco industry has unjustly enriched itself while distracting and confusing smokers about the harms and addictiveness of their product,” the proposal says.

“The industry has not been forced to bear the full costs of the harm caused by their product. These costs have either been borne by smokers themselves, or by taxpayers when smokers get sick and receive publicly funded or subsidised health care.”

A BAT Australia spokesperson said the company does not comment on potential or pending legal claims, while Philip Morris and Imperial Brands did not respond to requests for comment.

Francey told Guardian Australia that the proposal excludes the Northern Territory and the ACT, as the territories are an arm of the commonwealth, and there are differences in healthcare funding arrangements that could complicate the case.

The proposal seeks to recover healthcare costs incurred by the states since 2000, when internal tobacco industry documents were published revealing the industry knew that smoking caused serious diseases but colluded to cover up and obfuscate the evidence.

“I think you can justify a figure in the order of fifty billion, possibly even more,” Francey said.

In 1991, Francey represented consumers in a federal court of Australia case triggered by a Tobacco Institute of Australia advertisement that claimed there was “nothing which proves scientifically that cigarette smoke causes disease in nonsmokers”.

The court found compelling scientific proof that passive smoking causes lung disease and respiratory conditions in non-smokers, making the industry’s claims unlawful. The historic ruling accelerated workplace and public indoor smoking bans.

Francey said his latest proposal has the benefit of being brought by state governments under consumer protection laws, bypassing some of the challenges faced by smokers pursuing personal injury lawsuits, where it can be hard to prove which brand caused the harm, and with tobacco companies arguing people have “freedom of choice”.

Francey said state governments could seek court orders against companies engaged in misleading and deceptive conduct which has led to loss and damage and the likelihood of suffering in future.

The South Australian health minister, Blair Boyer, said there was a “substantial” public interest in measures reducing the harms that tobacco-related diseases place on governments, health systems and communities.

“While this proposal draws on historic findings regarding misleading and deceptive conduct by the tobacco industry, it is important that the state does its own due diligence,” he said.

“I have sought advice on the proposal, the likelihood of success and the benefits to South Australians, which will allow the government to consider its options.”

A spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said: “We will review his proposal carefully”.

A spokesperson for the Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, confirmed a meeting with Francey, but said the state was focused on laws targeting the illicit tobacco and vape trade. The Western Australian health minister, Meredith Hammat, said the state’s efforts are currently focused on strengthening tobacco legislation and enforcement activities.

The CEO of the Australian Council on Smoking & Health, Laura Hunter, said it would be “entirely reasonable for tobacco companies to bear the costs of the harm their products have caused” in Australia.

“For years, they’ve made money selling products that addict people and cause serious illness and death,” she said. “The responsibility for addressing that harm belongs with the companies that profited from it.”

The legal push follows cases overseas, including the landmark 1998 Master Settlement Agreement signed by major US tobacco companies and state attorneys general to settle dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover billions in smoking-related healthcare costs.

In 2025, three of the biggest tobacco companies were ordered to pay billions in compensation for smoking-related harms in Canada, though health groups expressed disappointment that the decision did not address harms from future use.

A professor of tobacco control with the University of Sydney, Becky Freeman, said the Canadian case was protracted over many years, and that any country taking on tobacco companies needed to ensure they were on “solid ground” to avoid spiralling costs and lacklustre outcomes.

“I am absolutely supportive of the tobacco industry being held accountable,” she said.

“I would want to ensure any action was comprehensive.”

Associate Prof Jonathan Liberman, an expert in law and global health at the University of Melbourne who has spent more than two decades working on legal aspects of tobacco control, said what has made tobacco litigation challenging is the scale and duration of the tobacco industry’s wrongdoing, and how vigorously the industry has defended it.

A range of features of the US legal system make large-scale litigation easier there, he said. To be successful in Australia, litigation against the tobacco industry over the health costs of smoking would need specific enabling legislation, and well resourced law firms working outside government doing the bulk of the necessary legal work, he said.

“Without these, lawsuits risk consuming significant time and public resources that may be better directed toward direct policy reform, and ultimately falling over on a combination of procedural grounds and resources running out.”

articles.title: Nigeria's president launches re-election manifesto but can he regain voters' trust?
articles.summary: For Nigerians to feel meaningful improvements, reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined, analysts say.
articles.preview: Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages. The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes. Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.

The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.

Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.

Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.

The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.

The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.

"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.

"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.

Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.

In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.

However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.

"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.

The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.

Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.

Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.

However, he has recently said he will work to reduce fuel cost.

His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.

Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.

"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.

However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.

"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.

While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.

Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.

"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.

To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.

But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.

Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.

"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."

To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.

"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.

Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.

He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.

"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.

Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.

"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Nigeria's power sector has suffered from years of underinvestment. The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.

Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.

The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.

"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.

Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.

The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.

For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.

"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.

"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.

Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.

"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.

As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge: building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.

"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.

"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

articles.body:
Naim Qassem says Republican losses and Israel’s election result could help Lebanon maintain sovereignty.

Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has welcomed Republican setbacks in US midterm elections last week and a lacklustre showing for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli polls, calling them a boon for Lebanon.

During a speech on Wednesday honouring members of the group killed by Israel, along with their families, Qassem described the elections in the US as an “earthquake” and the Israeli elections as a “defeat”. The bloc of Netanyahu, an arch-nemesis of the group, fell short of the 61 seats it needed to stay in power after the October 27 vote.

Qassem said the results were good for Lebanon and a signal that the country should resist the Trump administration’s push to disarm the group.

“Come, let us rebuild our country together, save it from the darkness of failure, and protect it from the empty rhetoric of those who sow discord and those who rely on American tutelage,” he said in a video-link address.

“Lebanon belongs to all of us. We are partners in building it and sharing the cost of protecting its sovereignty.”

Retaining Hezbollah arsenal

Iran-backed Hezbollah is locked in a standoff with US-backed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun over whether it will relinquish its arms, in a move Washington seeks but the group says would be a surrender to Israel.

The Hezbollah leader insisted it would not hand over its weapons and cited a continued Israeli military occupation over parts of the country’s south.

“There will be no state monopoly on the resistance’s weapons, no regulation, no prohibition, and no disarmament under Israeli occupation,” Qassem said.

The secretary-general assumed the role after Israel assassinated former Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah and his successor Hashem Safieddine in 2024.

Sparking months of ongoing war, the US and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran in February, assassinating Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah’s retaliation by firing missiles and drones into Israel led to weeks of intense Israeli strikes on south Lebanon, in which more than 4,300 people were killed, Lebanese authorities say, and around a million were displaced, according to the United Nations.

Qassem praised Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz for causing a spike in global oil prices and suspending shipping routes, saying it would weaken American and Israeli influence in the region.

US President Donald Trump has also acknowledged the role of the Iran war and the rise in fuel prices it stoked in last week’s electoral drubbing for Republicans, as did US Vice President and likely 2028 electoral hopeful JD Vance.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance said last week.

Conditions for disarmament

Qassem also warned against Lebanese authorities making commitments and deals that serve Israeli goals and urged them to focus on domestic issues.

“Why are you binding yourselves before the world to positions that serve the Israeli project?” he asked.

Israel continues to occupy large swathes of southern Lebanon and has decimated dozens of the roughly 60 villages and towns it occupies.

Although Israel and Lebanon negotiated a ceasefire with US mediation in June, Israel continues to bomb south Lebanon.

articles.preview: Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the joint intelligence committee, will take on the role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
articles.body:
The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe.

Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.”

This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely.

Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down.

“We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world.

Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job.

But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. The government is mulling a major weakening of targets for electric vehicles and has given the green light to a gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea while considering a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

“What we’re seeing in part is double standards,” Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, told the Guardian. “We can’t have Britain preaching a clean development gospel but expanding fossil fuels back at home. You cannot expect one set of rules for Africa and another for Britain.”

The UK’s credibility was “crumbling”, said Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “The prime minister’s first climate talks should be an opportunity to demonstrate he means business. But if this is all the UK has to offer, then the questions piling in about his climate credibility are more than justified.”

Under Alessandri, the JIC collaborated on a secret report warning that within five years the UK could begin experiencing national security impacts from the collapse of ecosystems overseas, driven by the climate crisis and overexploitation of the living world. These impacts included food shortages, rising food prices, mass migration and conflict among nuclear-armed countries.

The report was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer, but its contents were revealed by the Guardian last year, ahead of a redacted publication earlier this year.

Dame Madeleine Alessandri said: “Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates, placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world.

“The best time to address these risks is before they develop into crises. In this role, I will work with partners across government and internationally to strengthen our understanding of climate threats, build resilience and ensure we are better prepared for the challenges ahead.”

The risks of the climate crisis to national security were also highlighted by Ed Miliband, foreign secretary, who has been briefing foreign capitals on the findings of the JIC report. He is also at Cop31 this week, and told the Guardian: “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action – the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news.”

He added: “Climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face: food security, threats to infrastructure and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis].

“Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

In common with many wealthy nations, the UK has significantly rolled back its climate finance, funnelling money instead to military spending. In July, Burnham fronted a pledge to lower the cap on UK bus fares, funded by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

Prakash Dahal of Pro Public and Friends of the Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country’s adaptation to climate breakdown, and recovery from disasters such as the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal in August. “Crucially, this essential funding must come as grants – not loans,” he said. “Nepal is not asking for charity. Nepal is demanding justice.”

articles.title: Commentary: Melaka votes, Putrajaya watches - the hotly contested state polls could be harbinger of next Malaysia GE
articles.summary: The upcoming state poll is not really about Melaka. It is a testbed where Malaysia’s warring political parties will experiment with new alliances that are set to determine the shape of the next general election, writes CNA’s Leslie Lopez.
articles.preview: The upcoming state poll is not really about Melaka. It is a testbed where Malaysia’s warring political parties will experiment with new alliances that are set to determine the shape of the next general election, writes CNA’s Leslie Lopez. KUALA LUMPUR: For one of Malaysia’s smallest states, Melaka has been punching well above its weight in the country’s drawn-out political chaos. Following the 2018 general election, two state administrations collapsed in one term.
articles.body:
The upcoming state poll is not really about Melaka. It is a testbed where Malaysia’s warring political parties will experiment with new alliances that are set to determine the shape of the next general election, writes CNA’s Leslie Lopez.

KUALA LUMPUR: For one of Malaysia’s smallest states, Melaka has been punching well above its weight in the country’s drawn-out political chaos.

Following the 2018 general election, two state administrations collapsed in one term.

The Pakatan Harapan (PH) administration headed by then chief minister Adly Zahari fell in March 2020, weeks after the so-called Sheraton Move – the hotel-suite coup in which defecting Members of Parliament (MPs) toppled the PH federal government led by Mahathir Mohamad.

The incoming Barisan Nasional (BN) administration was itself later toppled in October 2021 when four assemblymen withdrew support. The snap state election that followed in November produced pitched three-way contests for the dominant ethnic Malay vote, in which BN prevailed. Thirteen of the state’s 28 state assembly seats were won by under one thousand votes.

When Melaka goes to the polls again on Saturday (Nov 14), the factors that produced the earlier havoc will no longer be in play.

The BN coalition, led by the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), and the Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, currently dominated by Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS), are campaigning as allies in a seat-sharing pact.

The PH coalition, on the other hand, appears to have an informal arrangement with Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu), the party behind the Sheraton Move that brought down the PH government in the first place.

In the coming days, all eyes will be on Melaka, especially at the administrative capital of Putrajaya, where strains between the components of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Unity Government are being discussed openly in coffeeshops and the corridors of Parliament.

FULL DRESS REHEARSAL

Melaka’s Saturday election has drawn 79 candidates into 11 straight fights, 11 three-cornered contests and six in four-cornered brawls for the 28 seats.

At stake is not just who will control the Melaka state government. The state has become the stage for a full dress rehearsal to Malaysia’s 16th general election, which is due sometime in early 2028 but widely expected in the next 12 months.

The headline experiment is the UMNO-PAS axis operating under the BN-PN banner. After knifing each other in previous electoral contests for the Malay vote, the BN coalition will contest in 23 seats, with UMNO running in 18 of them, and the PN coalition in five. There is zero overlap.

FUEL FOR AN EARLY GENERAL ELECTION

For Mr Anwar's PH, which held five seats before dissolution and is contesting in 24 state assembly constituencies in the upcoming polls, the situation is more grim.

PH’s survival strategy is based on an alliance it barely wants to acknowledge publicly and to which its main coalition partner, the Democratic Action Party (DAP), is openly uneasy about.

Should PH emerge from Melaka with fewer than five seats, the narrative that will dominate the weeks after is of Mr Anwar’s shrinking political mandate.

PH has already suffered state election defeats in Johor and Negeri Sembilan this year and a third consecutive drubbing in Melaka would revive questions about the coalition’s pull among Malay voters. That, in turn, would further weaken Mr Anwar’s hand within his own unity government.

Conversely, a comfortable PH-Bersatu showing would do the opposite by validating Mr Anwar’s coalition management and strengthen his hand to call for national polls at a time of his own choosing.

A THIRD FORCE ON TRIAL

Then there is Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama), a splinter from Mr Anwar’s Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) led by former PKR deputy president Rafizi Ramli.

The question hanging over Bersama is whether it can become a sustained third force.

The party, which Rafizi launched in May after taking over an obscure Penang-registered party, isn’t expected to win any seats. Bersama’s actual debut was in the July Johor state election, where it suffered a wipeout with all of its 15 candidates losing their deposits.

But Melaka could be different.

Bersama is contesting in 16 seats and its stated goal is modest: keeping its electoral deposits, which requires securing 12.5 per cent of the votes cast in contested areas.

The party unveiled its candidates back in August, two months before nomination days to give its unknown faces time to work the ground and present a new brand.

Melaka’s electorate has ballooned to over 680,000 from 495,000 in 2021, with the new voters made up of largely young Malaysians, who hold no allegiances. That is precisely the demographic Bersama’s data-driven and policy-heavy pitch is engineered to appeal to.

Bersama’s Melaka manifesto that was launched on Nov 2, includes channeling at least 30 per cent of the state operating expenditure - equivalent to over RM86 million (US$21.1 million) based on the 2024 budget - into direct-to-the-people programmes and a freeze on sea reclamation approvals.

If Bersama draws meaningfully from the urban, reform-minded Malays who once backed PKR and PH, it could establish itself as a credible protest vehicle ahead of the next general election.

But then again, Malaysia’s political graveyard is filled with wannabe third forces, which are now either defunct or effectively dead.

Among them include Semangat 46, which was founded by Tengku Razaleigh Hamzah as a breakaway from UMNO in the late 1980s. It was dissolved in 1996 and Tengku Razaleign returned to UMNO.

To be sure, state elections are imperfect federal barometers because voters reward and punish differently in these contests, especially when no prime minister is on the ballot.

Whatever the case, the results and data after Melaka votes will be mined seat for seat for clues over what could shape outcomes for GE16.

articles.body:
Uganda

A succession battle is emerging within Uganda’s ruling party, after senior officials rejected President Yoweri Museveni’s reported plan to position his son as his successor.

Five party sources say the proposal to back army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba was met with strong opposition during a closed-door meeting on Tuesday.

The vote was abandoned after several members spoke out against his candidacy, with only four reportedly voting in his favour and three against.

Kainerugaba, 52, has attracted controversy over inflammatory social media posts, including threats against political opponents and claims of torture.

He has also vowed to run for president in 2031.

Some party officials reportedly urged Museveni to move his son out of the army and give him a civilian role to build political experience.

Others suggested the 82-year-old president should seek another term instead.

Museveni has ruled Uganda since 1986, and the reported resistance marks an unusual challenge to his influence within the ruling party.

articles.title: F1 champion Lewis Hamilton calls on Israel to open Gaza’s Rafah border
articles.summary: Hamilton visited the Egypt-Gaza border as conditions worsened for Palestinians in Gaza after heavy rains.
articles.preview: Hamilton visited the Egypt-Gaza border as conditions worsened for Palestinians in Gaza after heavy rains. Lewis Hamilton visits Rafah crossing to witness Gaza aid efforts Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has called on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing to allow humanitarian supplies into Gaza from Egypt, amid worsening conditions after heavy rains and flooded makeshift camps.
articles.body:
Hamilton visited the Egypt-Gaza border as conditions worsened for Palestinians in Gaza after heavy rains.

Lewis Hamilton visits Rafah crossing to witness Gaza aid efforts

Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has called on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing to allow humanitarian supplies into Gaza from Egypt, amid worsening conditions after heavy rains and flooded makeshift camps.

The remarks came on Wednesday, a day after the British F1 driver visited Egypt’s northern city of el-Arish, which borders Gaza, touring a storage facility where the Egyptian Red Crescent had prepared boxes of aid to be sent to Palestinians in the besieged enclave.

In a post on social media, Hamilton said, “People in Gaza and Palestine are in such urgent need that they could hardly need this aid more than they do right now.”

“That’s why we really need to put pressure on Israel and work together to make sure this aid reaches them,” he said.

Hamilton said there were warehouses storing essential supplies in several locations, but the supplies were not reaching Palestinians who need them because of the border closure.

“Injustice”

A post on Hamilton’s Instagram page showed him meeting some of the volunteers and workers for the Egyptian Red Crescent, as well as stationary trucks loaded with food waiting to cross the border.

“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an injustice for people to being denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less,” Hamilton said.

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected accusations that Israel has been delaying the entry of winter supplies into the Gaza Strip.

More than 150,000 tents bought by humanitarian partners and member states are waiting outside the Gaza Strip for Israeli permission to enter, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said on Wednesday that waiting for a new Israeli government to form is “not an acceptable excuse” for delays in getting essential winter supplies into Gaza.

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title: United States warns Madagascar over growing security ties with Russia
articles.summary: The deputy head of US Africa Command said similar partnerships with military-led governments in Africa have failed to improve security.
articles.preview: Madagascar The United States has warned Madagascar against strengthening its military ties with Russia. The deputy head of US Africa Command (AFRICOM) cautioned that similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security. Lieutenant General John Brennan said they were concerned that Russia wants to expand the model it has used in the Sahel to elsewhere across the continent.
articles.body:
Madagascar

The United States has warned Madagascar against strengthening its military ties with Russia.

The deputy head of US Africa Command (AFRICOM) cautioned that similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.

Lieutenant General John Brennan said they were concerned that Russia wants to expand the model it has used in the Sahel to elsewhere across the continent.

"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.

Brennan highlighted the strategic value of the Mozambique Channel, the shipping route between those two countries, calling it vital to international trade.

The waterway has become more important as the Middle East war forces shipping through different routes.

Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso, all under military rule, have turned to Russia for support in their fight against jihadist groups, distancing themselves from Western partners.

Brennan's comments came as Madagascar's military government also deepens ties with Moscow.

Russia has expanded its cooperation with the island nation since the army seized power last year, supplying it with weapons and instructors from its paramilitary force, Africa Corps.

In one of Colonel Michael Randrianirina’s first official visits after seizing power, he travelled to Moscow on a plane chartered by Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Brennan said that while US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish", they should understand "the risks associated with that”.

He described Moscow’s approach as "largely ineffective" in the Sahel and east Africa, warning it could further destabilise the region if replicated elsewhere.

Brennan said he believed Russia’s "real motives" were to "control their natural resources, predate on their population, and then infringe on their sovereignty".

articles.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice says the men were involved in a string of plots, including a major incident near the UK airbase that is used by US armed forces.
articles.preview: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed. The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris.
articles.body:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.

Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment.

Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The BBC has asked the DOJ for comment on the suspected whereabouts of the two men not in US custody.

In the DOJ's statement detailing the indictments, it said: "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK."

It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

The indictment also details an arson attack on a Jewish charity in London on 17 April, which allegedly saw al-Hassani "directing" an individual over FaceTime.

On 17 April , a building previously used by Jewish Futures, an educational charity, was set alight in Hendon, north-west London.

The following day, the DOJ said al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London.

On 18 April, Kenton United Synagogue in Harrow was targeted in an arson attack. A 17-year-old boy pleaded guilty to the incident earlier this year.

The indictment also claims the three were involved in attacks on the Bank of New York Mellon building in Amsterdam on 15 March and on the Bank of America building in Paris on 28 March.

It added that the trio tried to carry out attacks on "Jewish institutions in the US", including attempting to target a synagogue in Manhattan, New York in March or April.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

RAF Fairford

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

articles.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
articles.preview: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power. It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid. The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
articles.body:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.

It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.

The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.title: Brazil electoral court fines Meta, sees no deliberate election bias
articles.summary: The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations."
articles.preview: Brazil's electoral court fines Meta $1.3M for noncompliance November 11, 2026 The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations." Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.
articles.body:
Brazil's electoral court fines Meta $1.3M for noncompliance

November 11, 2026

The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations."

Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.

However, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome.

Ahead of the runoff vote on October 25, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition filed a complaint, accusing Meta of "algorithmic manipulation" favoring his far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro.

Platforms owned by Meta include Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Meta told the court last month that it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns.

Meta lacked transparency, court says

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on Tuesday to impose the 7.5 million reais fine on the US tech giant.

Meta missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation, the court said.

On the other hand, the court's reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there were no preliminary evidence indicating that any intentional actions were taken to influence the election.

"That conclusion would require robust evidence, to be produced through the appropriate legal proceedings," he said.

According to Bellizze, the fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders, including delays, incomplete disclosures, and challenges in verifying some of the information it provided.

In a statement on Wednesday, Meta strongly denied the court's ruling.

"We will continue to present the facts and defend ourselves against false allegations in the ongoing legal proceedings," Meta said in a statement on Wednesday.

Lula vows to rein in social media

Lula defeated Bolsonaro in a tight run-off in October 25 with him winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.2%.

In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race.

"We had to overcome foreign interference in the election, coming from outside through digital platforms that we will have to regulate," he said.

Lieutenant General John Brennan, deputy commander of US Africa Command, said Washington was concerned that Russia could extend its influence beyond the Sahel, where military-led governments have increasingly turned to Moscow for security assistance.

Russia has supplied Madagascar with weapons and military instructors since the country's military takeover in 2025.

President Michaël Randrianirina has continued to pursue closer relations with Moscow. The two countries recently signed agreements covering defence, trade and tourism during a Russia-Africa summit.

Randrianirina also travelled to Moscow in February, marking the first official visit by a Malagasy leader in nearly five decades.

Madagascar has not publicly responded to the US warning.

articles.title: Iran designates Argentinian navy, air force as ‘terrorist organisations’
articles.summary: The move comes months after the government of Javier Milei designated Iran's IRGC as a 'terrorist organisation'.
articles.preview: The move comes months after the government of Javier Milei designated Iran’s IRGC as a ‘terrorist organisation’. The government of Iran has announced it will designate the naval and air forces of Argentina as “terrorist organisations”, in a tit-for-tat response to how the South American country designated its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in March. Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday that it considers the two branches of the Argentinian military “terrorist organisations” by “the principle of reciprocity”.
articles.body:
The move comes months after the government of Javier Milei designated Iran’s IRGC as a ‘terrorist organisation’.

The government of Iran has announced it will designate the naval and air forces of Argentina as “terrorist organisations”, in a tit-for-tat response to how the South American country designated its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in March.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday that it considers the two branches of the Argentinian military “terrorist organisations” by “the principle of reciprocity”. The statement does not mention Argentina’s army.

“It is evident that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government,” the statement adds.

Argentina’s foreign ministry responded with a statement of its own saying that it “categorically rejects” Iran’s designation.

“This measure is completely baseless and constitutes an unacceptable accusation,” the statement reads.

Wednesday’s back-and-forth, however, is not the first time that relations between Iran and Argentina have been strained.

Argentina blames the Iran-backed group Hezbollah for a deadly bombing attack on the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires in 1994, which killed 85 people and injured hundreds more.

The office of Argentinian President Javier Milei referenced that incident on March 31, when it issued the “terrorist” designation against the IRGC.

“President Javier Milei hopes this decision will settle a historical debt of more than 30 years with the families of the victims,” a statement from his office said at the time.

“This government is determined to bring the Argentine Republic back into alignment with Western civilization, while condemning and directly combating those who seek to destroy it.”

The decision to designate the IRGC as a “terrorist organisation” also aligned with a push under United States President Donald Trump to isolate Iran.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, and the two countries have called on international allies to support their offensive.

While many leaders in Latin America have avoided taking sides in global conflicts, Milei has positioned his government firmly behind the US and Israel.

Milei’s abrasive style has sometimes brought him into conflict with other countries in the region, including key regional economic players like Brazil.

The Argentinian leader has also revived his country’s dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, which his country refers to as Las Malvinas and claims as part of its national territory.

articles.title: Hormuz Strait will ‘never return’ to pre-war status, Iran’s Ghalibaf says
articles.summary: Iran's parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions.
articles.preview: Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions for ending war. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran. In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict.
articles.body:
Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions for ending war.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran.

In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict.

“There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he said.

Seven conditions

Ghalibaf said Tehran provided a clear response to the US through a Qatari mediator that included its seven conditions for peace talks, adding that Iran is waiting for an official response.

“The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Iran’s conditions, as outlined by the chief negotiator, include lifting the US-imposed naval blockade and sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

He said these demands were part of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and their implementation was necessary before entering negotiations with the US.

“If America limits itself to what has been agreed upon without making excessive demands or engaging in behaviour that breeds distrust, then, naturally, reaching an agreement is possible,” he said.

“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States.”

Renewed conflict

Ghalibaf said US officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to mediate direct negotiations with Tehran during a visit to Moscow.

He warned against new US attacks against Iran, saying that US President Donald Trump will face another defeat and political pressure from the new Congress that takes office in January.

Iran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, he said, urging a sustainable deterrent capability, including military capabilities.

Yemen mediation

On the ongoing fighting in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for “Supporters of God”), Ghalibaf said that “no one should interfere” in it.

“If both the government in Yemen and Saudi Arabia were to ask for our help, we would certainly offer our assistance to help resolve their conflict,” he said.

Iran has previously offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group in October following a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

articles.title: Nelle scuole un attacco ibrido 'con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia'
articles.summary: Criminologo Sapienza ed esperto Ue: 'minaccia immateriale che mina la fiducia sociale'
articles.preview: 'Un attacco ibrido con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia: "un attacco di questo tipo è diverso dalla guerra ibrida e non è nemmeno terrorismo: è una minaccia immateriale che ha conseguenze a livello sociale, cognitivo e istituzionale. Sfrutta cioè il funzionamento ordinario della società per moltiplicare un effetto destabilizzante", dice all'ANSA Arije Antinori, professore di Criminologia alla Sapienza Università di Roma ed esperto dell'Eu Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation (Eukh), l'iniziativa della Commissione Europea lanciata nel 2024…
articles.body:
'Un attacco ibrido con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia: "un attacco di questo tipo è diverso dalla guerra ibrida e non è nemmeno terrorismo: è una minaccia immateriale che ha conseguenze a livello sociale, cognitivo e istituzionale. Sfrutta cioè il funzionamento ordinario della società per moltiplicare un effetto destabilizzante", dice all'ANSA Arije Antinori, professore di Criminologia alla Sapienza Università di Roma ed esperto dell'Eu Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation (Eukh), l'iniziativa della Commissione Europea lanciata nel 2024 per contrastare estremismo violento e terrorismo negli Stati membri.

La scelta delle scuole come obiettivo, osserva , "è determinante perché la scuola è la porta d'ingresso di un sistema interdipendente costituito da famiglie, istituzioni, media e opinione pubblica, che si sorreggono attraverso un rapporto di fiducia". Attacchi a costo limitato come questi colpiscono, "il sistema di relazioni" e "sovraccaricano le istituzioni di compiti". In pratica, si attacca la sicurezza della vita quotidiama. Questa, osserva Antinori, "dipende da presupposti che raramente vengono messi in discussione. Per esempio, per tutti la scuola è un luogo protetto, le emergenze sono percepite come eventi sporadici, ci si fida delle comunicazioni ufficiali". Gli attacchi ibridi "non solo diffondono paura e incertezza, ma fanno in modo che l'insicurezza venga percepita come un fatto ordinario: così si colpisce il sistema di relazioni interno alla società". Le conseguenze, rileva , hanno una "portata sistemica": attaccando il sistema di relazioni ,ottengono un effetto destabilizzante e generano "una perturbazione sociale che mina le relazioni di fiducia".

Il problema più grande degli attacchi ibridi, prosegue Antinori, "è che una volta evidenziate le vulnerabilità, altri attori possono sfruttare la situazione con attacchi opportunistici ibridi" verso obiettivi legati alla quotidianità, come è avvenuto recentemente in voli di linea, supermercati e scuole. Se qualcuno innesca l'attacco, altri possono intervenire successivamente, compresi gruppi della criminalità organizzata, fino a "indebolire e sfilacciare il tessuto sociale delle democrazie all'interno", osserva.

Se le infrastrutture critiche tradizionali erano energia luce, gas, acqua o connessioni internet, per gli attacchi ibridi "tutto ciò che è legato alla quotidianità può diventare un'infrastruttura critica, con i conseguenti costi operativi di gestione e sicurezza". Si tende a "mandare in crisi il nostro sistema fino a indurci a fare passi indietro nei processi democratici". E' una situazione che nessuno Stato, nemmeno i più avanzati, è in grado di governare. Reagire è possibile "lavorando moltissimo sul piano della resilienza, ripristinando un contesto di fiducia nella comunità in modo forte e considerando la disinformazione una minaccia sul piano politico". Bisogna prepararsi, conclude l'esperto, perché in futuro attacchi come quelli recenti potrebbero colpire anche in un'unica giornata.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
articles.preview: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day. Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion. However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
articles.body:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.

Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."
